description: Bertrand and Mullainathan sent nearly 5,000 fictitious resumes to help-wanted ads in Boston and Chicago, half with white-sounding names and half with African-American-sounding names. White names received 50% more callbacks. Applicants with white names needed about 10 resumes per callback; those with African-American names needed about 15.
energy_note: Fifty per cent more callbacks, for the name alone.

description: For white names a higher-quality resume produced 30% more callbacks. For African-American names it produced a far smaller increase. Improving the CV does not close the gap, which means the usual advice does not work.
energy_note: Getting better qualified helps them more than it helps you.

description: Federal contractors, larger employers and employers explicitly stating they are Equal Opportunity Employers did not treat the African-American resumes more favourably.
energy_note: The declaration on the advert made no measurable difference.

description: A meta-analysis of field experiments found the trend since 1990 close to flat, sloping slightly upward - no change in the rate of discrimination against African Americans over three decades.
energy_note: Thirty years of measurement, and a flat line.

description: Callbacks are not hires, so the effect cannot be converted directly into earnings. Darolia et al. argue many audits overstate discrimination by using very stereotypical names, and found no callback gap when pairing typically-white first names with typically-black surnames. Recorded because the counter-evidence belongs in the row.
energy_note: Strong finding, real methodological dispute, both stated.

aspect: Which is why people change the name
description: Shortening, anglicising, or using a middle name measurably improves callbacks and costs something that is not measured anywhere.
energy_note: Getting the interview by not being yourself.
